NEWBORN 2 · LESSON 2

Faces & Visual Tracking for Babies 6–12 Weeks

Age 6–12 WeeksSubject SeeClass Newborn 2Duration 2–5 minutes

Between 6 and 12 weeks, your baby starts to hold a gaze a little longer and follows movement with their eyes. This class uses simple high-contrast faces, gentle patterns and a first taste of strong colour — twelve cards you show one at a time, in a calm two-to-five-minute session whenever it suits you both.

Faces are a baby’s favourite thing to look at, and moving a card slowly from side to side turns that looking into early visual tracking practice. Nothing to teach and nothing to test — just an easy next step from your first class.

PARENT INSTRUCTIONS

How to use this activity

Choose a time when your baby is awake, calm and comfortable. Hold the card where your baby can comfortably see it and allow time to look. For tracking activities, move the card slowly from side to side. There is no need to complete every card in one session. Stop when your baby looks away, becomes tired or loses interest.

At this stage, Kiddo School introduces simple faces, high-contrast patterns and a small amount of strong color.

Every baby develops differently. Kiddo School age ranges are guides, not tests or developmental deadlines.

    Eyes — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

    This lesson turns the eyes card into a calm two-to-five-minute session: where to hold it, what to say, and which tiny baby responses count as real work.

    What is this?

    Eyes are the part of the face people look with — and at 6–12 weeks they are also the part of YOUR face your baby finds most magnetic. The card puts two big friendly eyes in bold black and white, the easiest thing for brand-new vision to lock onto.

    What does it mean?

    Newborn sight is blurry except at close range, and dark bold shapes against white give the sharpest signal available. Eyes sit inside that sweet spot: high contrast, face-shaped, and usually attached to someone who loves your baby.

    What does the child need to know?

    Hold the card 20–30 cm away — about the distance from your elbow to your fingertips, where baby vision focuses best. Expect staring, going still, small starts and quick glances away; all of it is working, not boredom.

    Why this matters

    Looking at eyes is the first step of every conversation your baby will ever have. Eye contact feeds bonding, and every second of steady fixation exercises the eye muscles that tracking, focusing and, years later, reading will be built on.

    What it teaches

    Visual fixation (holding a gaze), early attention, eye-muscle control, and the social loop — look, be looked back at — that all conversation grows from.

    Words to learn

    eyeslookblinkhellofacepeek

    Say this to your child

    “"Look, eyes. Two big eyes looking at you. Here are my eyes — I am blinking, blink, blink. Hello, little one. Your eyes and my eyes are saying hello."”

    Step by step

    1. Settle your baby in your lap or lying alert on a firm surface, then show the card at elbow-to-fingertips distance, straight in the line of sight.
    2. Name it warmly and slowly: "Eyes. Look — eyes." Two or three times is plenty; the words ride on your voice, not the other way round.
    3. Go quiet and watch. Fixation may last seconds or a minute; either way your baby is aiming their gaze, and that aiming is the whole skill.
    4. Lean in so your own face sits beside the card and blink slowly — first the card’s pair, then yours, so your baby can compare.
    5. Finish at the first yawn, squirm or glance away, and jot down which response you saw; tomorrow you are watching for its repeat.

    Look closer at the picture

    The artwork is verified simple: two large eyes, stark black on white, nothing else on the card. Point out the round pupils and the curve of the lids — then turn to the more interesting artwork: your baby’s face.

    Ask your child

    Watch for: does the gaze lock on quickly or drift? Does a slow blink from you pull a blink or a startle back? Wonder aloud, to yourself or the baby: "I wonder which eyes you like best — the card’s or mine?"

    What your child can say or do

    Your baby might hold a long, unblinking stare, soften and still as they find your eyes, give a first wobbly smile, or look from card to you and back — the first version of checking something twice.

    Out in the real world

    Eyes are everywhere your baby looks: yours at every feed, a sibling’s across the bath, grandparents on a video call. Each time someone leans close and gets held in a gaze, the card is happening live.

    Try it together

    Peek-a-boo, newborn edition: hide your eyes behind your palm for one second, then uncover them with a soft "peek". At this age the reappearance itself is the joke — no sound effects needed.

    Understanding check

    A parent self-check: can you name the focusing distance for this age, and did you catch one clear moment of fixation or eye contact today? Two yeses and the lesson landed.

    Parent tips

    Short beats long: two minutes of real looking beats ten of tired glancing. If a session fizzles, try again after a nap rather than pushing on. The card is a prop; your face is the main event.

    Staying safe

    Keep sessions hands-on and supervised — a card near a newborn means a grown-up holding it, never propped in a cot or left within grabbing range. Choose calm, alert windows, and let looking away end things; an overstimulated baby needs quiet, not more input.

    This lesson pairs with the Eyes flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Faces & Visual Tracking (Newborn 2).

    Happy face — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

    Somewhere in these weeks many babies aim their first real smile at a face — this lesson shows you how to invite one with the happy face card, without ever demanding it.

    What is this?

    A happy face is a face with the mouth turned up. Babies meet smiles three ways at this age: the drawn one on the card, the ones you wear, and the brand-new ones they make themselves — social smiles aimed at people, not at wind or sleep.

    What does it mean?

    Between six and twelve weeks smiling stops being reflex and starts being social: your baby sees a face, feels good, and the mouth joins in. A bold high-contrast smile is easy to find and easy to imitate, which is why face cards have a reputation for pulling grins out.

    What does the child need to know?

    The three smiles worth telling apart: reflex (arrives in sleep, gone in a flash), wind (mid-feed, grimace-shaped), social (aimed at you or the card, slower, with bright eyes). Only the third is conversation, and it cannot be commanded — only invited.

    Why this matters

    A social smile is your baby’s first tool for holding an adult’s attention, and it works both ways: smiling releases the good feeling that makes looking, cooing and turn-taking worth repeating. It is the opening move of friendship.

    What it teaches

    Social-emotional bonding, facial imitation (the forerunner of all copying), visual discrimination of expressions, and turn-taking — smile, reply, smile again.

    Words to learn

    smilehappyhellofaceagainmy turn

    Say this to your child

    “"Happy face! Look at that big smile. I have a smile too — see? Can you find my smile? There it is. Hello, happy baby. Smiles go back and forth, all day long."”

    Step by step

    1. Pick an alert, fed, changed moment and show the card at focusing distance, smile-side up, where the light falls on it.
    2. Say its name slowly and warmly: "Happy face. What a big smile." Then simply let your baby look.
    3. Copy the card — hold the same wide smile on your own face and keep it there, so card and parent match.
    4. Watch the mouth corners. Any upward twitch, soft open-mouth look or full grin gets a delighted reply from you, out loud.
    5. End the moment while it is still sweet — one good smile, named and answered, is the whole class for the day.

    Look closer at the picture

    The artwork is a bold high-contrast smiley face — wide upturned mouth, simple open features, nothing busy behind it. Say what you see, then turn the noticing outward: which expression is your baby wearing right now?

    Ask your child

    Watch for the reply chain: does your smile earn one back? Does the card hold attention longer on some days than others? Wonder aloud: "I wonder if that smile was for me or for the card — I will try again after lunch."

    What your child can say or do

    You might get a full gummy grin aimed at the card, a slower sleepy smile for you, a kick of the legs, a coo, or a long studying stare with the smile arriving only when you copy the face — every version is a pass.

    Out in the real world

    Smiles travel through the whole day: the one that greets a sibling, the one that lands on grandma on a video call, the one your baby practises on the changing mat. Each one proves the card’s lesson — faces answer faces.

    Try it together

    Copy-cat faces: make three slow expressions — smile, wide-open surprise, tongue out — pausing ten seconds between each. You are not teaching expressions yet; you are showing your baby that faces are a game two people can play.

    Understanding check

    Quick parent self-check: did you spot one social smile today, and did you answer it out loud within a second or two? Answering promptly is the half of the skill that belongs to you.

    Parent tips

    Do not work for a smile — leaning in with a strained grin teaches effort, not warmth. A tired or overloaded baby may stare blankly; that is a no for now, not a no forever. Both parents, and any siblings, can run this lesson — more faces, more practice.

    Staying safe

    Hold the card yourself at all times and keep it out of the cot — a newborn cannot push a card off their face. If your baby turns away, arches or cries, end the session; fussing is how this age says the show is over.

    This lesson pairs with the Happy face flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Faces & Visual Tracking (Newborn 2).

    Different face — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

    Show this card beside the happy face over the week and your baby starts sorting the world’s first category: faces that are the same, and faces that are not.

    What is this?

    This card carries a second face whose expression differs from the smiling one. Side by side they make a tiny set — same idea, different face — and noticing that gap is the very beginning of comparing, sorting and preference.

    What does it mean?

    Babies do not need words to compare. When two images take turns in view, the brain tracks what stays (eyes, mouth, face shape) and what changes (the expression). That quiet bookkeeping is categorisation in its first clothes.

    What does the child need to know?

    You do not need to teach "same" and "different" — you only need to offer both cards across a few days. Preference is the evidence: many babies this age lock onto one face and give the other a glance, and either choice is a finding.

    Why this matters

    Every later skill — sorting socks, telling the cat from the dog, telling b from d — stands on this first distinction: things that look alike are not all alike. Faces are the friendliest place to start, because babies already care about them.

    What it teaches

    Visual discrimination, early comparison, memory for images seen before, and the social idea that different people wear different expressions.

    Words to learn

    facedifferentagainlookthis onethat one

    Say this to your child

    “"Two faces! This face and that face. They are not the same — look closely. One says hello with a big smile, and this one has a different thing to say. Which face is looking at you today?"”

    Step by step

    1. On day one, show only this card and name it plainly: "A different face. Hello, new face."
    2. On day two, bring the smiling card back and let your baby meet them in turn — one, then the other, with plenty of seconds apart.
    3. Hold the pair side by side at focusing distance and let the eyes travel; a slow sway of one card restarts the looking.
    4. Narrate the difference without teaching it: "This one smiles wide. This one looks different." Then stop talking and watch.
    5. Note which face wins the longer gaze and lead with that one next time — your baby’s preference is the syllabus now.

    Look closer at the picture

    The artwork shows a second bold face whose expression differs from the smiling one — same high-contrast style, different mood. Describe only that: the shape of the mouth, the feel of the look. The real experiment is your baby’s eyes, choosing.

    Ask your child

    Watch which card the gaze returns to after visiting both, and whether the return changes by day or by mood. Wonder aloud: "I wonder what makes you choose — the shape, or the one you saw first?"

    What your child can say or do

    Longer fixation on one face, a frown of concentration while comparing, a smile reserved for just one of the pair, or restless looking that means "too much" — all four are answers, and one of them is data.

    Out in the real world

    Difference fills the day: two grandparents with two voices, the family cat and the neighbour’s dog, your two hands. Naming pairs casually — "one shoe, other shoe" — keeps the comparing game running between sessions.

    Try it together

    Two-voice game: hold one card each side of your baby’s view and greet your baby in a different voice for each face — low and slow on the left, bright and quick on the right. Eyes and ears compare together.

    Understanding check

    Parent self-check: did the two cards actually meet this week, and did you catch which one held the longer look? If not yet, lay them out after the next nap — the comparing is your baby’s to do, not yours.

    Parent tips

    Resist labelling expressions beyond what you see ("grumpy", "naughty" and friends can wait years). Swap card order between days so position does not decide the winner. A blank day means nothing; preferences at this age are weather, not climate.

    Staying safe

    Keep both cards in adult hands and out of reach — at this age everything heads for the mouth eventually, and a soggy card grows mould. Session length stays short: two faces is a lot of information for twelve weeks.

    This lesson pairs with the Different face flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Faces & Visual Tracking (Newborn 2).

    Face pattern — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

    This card sits between the faces and the pure patterns in your set: features built from bold shapes. This lesson uses it to stretch your baby’s looking a few seconds longer.

    What is this?

    A face pattern is a face whose features are made of decorative shapes rather than plain circles and curves — half portrait, half design. For a baby it doubles the interest: the face pulls the gaze in, the patterns hold it there.

    What does it mean?

    Young attention is a muscle before it is a habit. Detailed images give it something to do: the eye travels from shape to shape, resting and restarting. Faces with built-in detail reliably stretch fixation past what a plain shape manages.

    What does the child need to know?

    Your finger is the tour guide here. Tracing slowly, one shape per visit, turns a still card into a moving one — and a moving target is what young eyes follow longest. Do not name every shape; "so many patterns!" carries the whole lesson.

    Why this matters

    Sustained attention at three months predicts nothing and promises nothing — but it practises something: the feeling of staying with one thing. That feeling is the raw material of every later puzzle, book and conversation.

    What it teaches

    Visual attention span, smooth eye travel across an image, shape interest, and calm shared focus — parent and baby attending to the same thing at the same time, which is joint attention in its earliest form.

    Words to learn

    patternsshapeslooktracelinesface

    Say this to your child

    “"Look at this face — it is made of patterns! Lines here, shapes there. My finger is going for a little walk... round and round, up and down. Look at all these patterns on one face."”

    Step by step

    1. Show the card at close range in good light and give it its name: "A pattern face. So many shapes."
    2. Let your baby find it alone first — ten seconds of free looking before you do anything at all.
    3. Then trace one pattern with your fingertip, slowly, from one end to the other, saying nothing or nearly nothing.
    4. Rest your finger, count three breaths, and trace a different shape — one tour at a time, no grand tours.
    5. Hand the session back to your baby: card still, voice quiet, and watch where the eyes wander next. That wandering is the workout.

    Look closer at the picture

    What the artwork verifiably shows: a face whose features are built from bold high-contrast shapes inside the outline. Name the shapes you actually see rather than inventing detail, and keep the richer question for the live picture — where do your baby’s eyes land first?

    Ask your child

    Watch the travel: do the eyes hop between shapes or slide? Does your tracing finger collect the gaze and lead it? Wonder aloud: "I wonder which shape is the favourite — I will start there tomorrow."

    What your child can say or do

    Fixation that outlasts the plainer cards, eyes that shadow your fingertip the whole way, a stillness that looks like study, or a sudden tired glance away — the last one is the honest finish line, not a failure.

    Out in the real world

    Patterns ride through the whole house: stripes on a shirt, tiles on the kitchen floor, the grill of the radiator. Wherever bold pattern meets your baby’s day, one slow trace with your finger re-runs this lesson in five seconds.

    Try it together

    Shape walk: lay two or three cards in a gentle arc at focusing distance and let your baby’s gaze travel the arc while you narrate the stops — "here... and here... and here." You are building the habit of looking around, not quizzing.

    Understanding check

    Ask yourself two things: did the looking last longer today than on a plainer card, and did you manage to stay quiet through at least one full trace? Both grow with practice — yours and the baby’s.

    Parent tips

    If your baby loses the card mid-trace, start the trace again from the top without comment; restarting is normal at this age. Keep your voice lower than you think it needs to be — quiet is what makes detail visible to a new brain.

    Staying safe

    Trace with a clean, dry hand — this card will spend its life near a newborn, and feeds happen fast. Lying-down sessions belong on a firm surface with you alongside; never leave a young baby propped with a card in reach.

    This lesson pairs with the Face pattern flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Faces & Visual Tracking (Newborn 2).

    Concentric circles — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

    This lesson uses the ring card two ways — still, for inward gaze practice, and moving, for the near-far rhythm babies find quietly amazing.

    What is this?

    Concentric circles are circles nested inside circles, like ripples from a dropped stone. Drawn in bold black and white they give a young baby one clear centre to aim at and a set of rings to travel inward through.

    What does it mean?

    Two visual jobs live in this card. The centre gives fixation a bullseye; the rings give the eye a path. Moving the whole card closer and further adds a third: focusing — the lens-work your baby’s eyes are only just learning to do.

    What does the child need to know?

    Stillness in a watching baby is not boredom — it is concentration at full volume. Some babies go completely quiet on this card. Give the stillness room, keep your voice low, and resist filling the silence with words.

    Why this matters

    Tracking and focusing are the twin skills under everything visual your baby will ever do. Rings offer both in the gentlest form: no corners to trip over, no story to follow, just in, in, in — and out again.

    What it teaches

    Fixation on a target, inward tracking, distance focusing, and self-regulation — the quiet alertness that lets looking become studying.

    Words to learn

    circlesroundinoutrippleslook

    Say this to your child

    “"Circles, inside circles, all the way in. Here is the middle — a tiny circle hiding inside the big ones. The circle comes closer... and further away. Round and round the rings go."”

    Step by step

    1. Show the card still and centred at focusing distance, and let the bullseye do its work — say its name once: "Circles. Round and round."
    2. Move the card slowly closer, then slowly further, about the length of your hand each way. The rings will seem to breathe.
    3. Watch the eyes adjust; some babies lean in, some go very still, some blink in a slow rhythm of their own.
    4. Trace one ring from outside in with your fingertip, one slow lap, and stop at the centre without a word.
    5. Finish on a look-away or a yawn, whichever comes first — this card is calm work, and calm work ends early.

    Look closer at the picture

    The artwork is verified simple: bold black and white rings, one inside another, nothing else on the card. Say that plainly, then watch the better show — your baby going still, which at this age is effort, not absence.

    Ask your child

    Watch for the lean: does your baby’s head tilt forward as the card comes closer? Does a blink or a sigh arrive when it pulls back? Wonder aloud: "I wonder if the stillness is looking or resting — after a nap I will find out."

    What your child can say or do

    Total stillness with wide eyes, a slow lean towards the card, soft cooing that matches your calm voice, or a heavy-lidded drift towards sleep — rings settle some babies so well they end their own session.

    Out in the real world

    Nested circles are rarer than you would think in a house — plates stacked on plates, the rings of a bath toy, lampshade circles one above the other. Wherever circles nest, one quiet "round and round" keeps the card’s idea alive.

    Try it together

    Ripple voice: hum one long low note while tracing ring after ring inward, letting the note fade as your finger reaches the centre. Sound winding down plus eyes travelling in makes a wind-down ritual worth keeping.

    Understanding check

    Parent check-in: did you manage one slow near-far move without hurrying, and did your baby give you ten quiet seconds of looking? That combination is the whole lesson; nothing else is owed today.

    Parent tips

    Move slower than feels natural — at this age, quick movement vanishes. If the stillness worries you, wave gently once; a response means an awake, working baby. Save this card for the wind-down end of a session, not the opener.

    Staying safe

    Near-far movement stays in your hand, never on a string or propped above the cot — an object swinging over a baby’s face is a grown-up job with eyes on it the whole time. Keep sessions to a few minutes; calm is the goal, mileage is not.

    This lesson pairs with the Concentric circles flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Faces & Visual Tracking (Newborn 2).

    LEARNING PATH LESSON · FACES & VISUAL TRACKING · AGES 6–12 WEEKS

    Wavy lines — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

    Waves are the friendly gatekeeper of tracking: smooth, corner-free and endlessly re-traceable. This lesson walks one wave at a time.

    What is this?

    Wavy lines are curves that rise and fall across the card, drawn thick and bold. For a baby whose eyes are learning to move on purpose, a wave is a road: it goes somewhere, and it never turns sharply.

    What does it mean?

    Smooth pursuit — the eye’s ability to follow a moving path — is assembled in these months from practice. Curves suit beginners because the direction change is gradual; the eye succeeds often, and success keeps the game alive.

    What does the child need to know?

    Take a single wave each lap, left to right, at a walking-in-honey pace. Your finger leads and the gaze follows; if the eyes drop off the line, pause and let them re-find it alone. Left-to-right order is a quiet gift to a future reader, not a rule to enforce.

    Why this matters

    Every look your baby will ever take — at a rolling ball, a passing bus, a line of text — runs on the eye control this card exercises. Waves make the practice feel like nothing, which is exactly why it works.

    What it teaches

    Smooth visual tracking, left-to-right scanning, hand-eye coordination when tracing, and shared rhythm — sway, trace, watch, repeat.

    Words to learn

    wavesupdownsideslowboat

    Say this to your child

    “"Waves! Up and down and up and down, slow as a boat on sleepy water. My finger rides the wave — here it goes, all the way across. And back again. One little wave at a time."”

    Step by step

    1. Show the card at focusing distance and name it with a rising-falling voice: "Wavy lines. Up... and down."
    2. Lay your fingertip at the start of one wave and travel it left to right, slower than slow, while your baby watches.
    3. At the end, rest, breathe once, and trace the same wave back — repetition is the interest here, not variety.
    4. Then sway the whole card gently side to side like a slow boat and let the whole image move as one.
    5. Trade jobs: still card plus moving finger, then moving card plus still voice. Whichever holds your baby longer wins tomorrow.

    Look closer at the picture

    The artwork shows bold wavy lines rolling across a plain card — that is all it claims, so say exactly that much. The tracing and the swaying are yours to add; the richness to notice is whether the eyes ride the line or hop off it.

    Ask your child

    Watch the ride: does the gaze stay with the finger to the end of the wave, or slip off mid-way? Does the boat-sway pull the eyes when the finger does not? Wonder aloud, softly: "Slower, or even slower — I wonder which you like."

    What your child can say or do

    Eyes gliding along with the finger, a whole-body wiggle when the card sways, a gummy attempt to bat at the moving line, or watching that ends in a yawn — a yawn on this card is a job well done, not a dropout.

    Out in the real world

    Waves live in daily life: the scalloped edge of a doily, the curved handle of a mug, water in the bath moving as your hand sweeps it. Trace any real curve you pass and the card keeps rehearsing itself.

    Try it together

    Boat lap: hold your baby supported against your shoulder and sway side to side in the same up-down rhythm as your tracing voice. Eyes, ears and body get one wave together — the fullest version of this lesson there is.

    Understanding check

    Two-question self-check: did one wave get traced all the way across at least once, and did the eyes follow for most of the trip? If yes on both, the tracking practice happened — done for today.

    Parent tips

    Trace with the hand your baby sees best from their current position, and swap sides across the week so both eyes get equal work. If interest fades fast, do a single wave and stop; short and perfect beats long and sloppy.

    Staying safe

    Sway small and slow — a young baby’s neck does most of the holding at this age, so big movements belong to the card, not the baby. Keep the card a hand’s width from the face during swaying so it never taps or covers them.

    This lesson pairs with the Wavy lines flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Faces & Visual Tracking (Newborn 2).

    Zigzag — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

    After the smooth waves, this card changes the rules: every corner is a small event. This lesson turns those events into a game of tick and tock.

    What is this?

    A zigzag is a line that turns sharply back and forth — corners instead of curves. Where the waves let the eye rest while it moved, the zigzag asks it to notice: the direction just changed, right there, at the point.

    What does it mean?

    Direction change is visual news. An eye that has learned curves now meets events, and each corner is a miniature surprise — expected once traced twice, exciting every time. Surprise, in small safe doses, is what keeps attention growing.

    What does the child need to know?

    Zigzags are busier than waves, and busy burns attention faster. Expect a shorter visit and treat that as normal. The tick-tock trick — a tiny voice turn at every corner — marks the changes so the eyes learn to predict them.

    Why this matters

    The world does not move in curves only: hands reach and withdraw, siblings dart, pets turn on a sixpence. An eye that has practised corners catches sudden movers sooner, and a baby who predicts the next turn is learning that the world has rules.

    What it teaches

    Visual scanning across direction changes, anticipation (what happens at the corner?), auditory-visual pairing through the tick-tock voice, and tolerance for gentle surprise.

    Words to learn

    zigzagcornerturnticktockpointy

    Say this to your child

    “"Zigzag — up to the corner, turn! Down to the corner, turn! Tick, tock, tick, tock. The line cannot decide which way to go, so it goes both ways. What a busy, pointy line."”

    Step by step

    1. Show the card briefly and name it with a playful voice: "Zigzag! Pointy corners everywhere."
    2. Trace the line slowly and let your voice tick at one corner and tock at the next — sound marks the surprise so it stops being a jolt.
    3. Pause at a corner, finger parked, and wait; some babies stare hardest exactly at the turn.
    4. Run the trace a second time at the same speed so the corners become predictable — prediction is the skill hiding in this card.
    5. Stop while curiosity is still alive; a shorter session on a busy card leaves the door open for tomorrow.

    Look closer at the picture

    The artwork is a thick zigzag line full of hard angles and about-turns — say that and no more. The real show to notice: does your baby’s gaze hesitate a beat at each corner? That hesitation is the surprise landing.

    Ask your child

    Watch the corners: do the eyes pause at the turns or sail across them? Does the tick-tock voice collect the gaze back after a slip? Wonder aloud: "I wonder if you knew the corner was coming by the third lap."

    What your child can say or do

    A stare pinned to one corner, a startle at the first turn that settles by the third, rapid eye-darting that mirrors the line, or a quick loss of interest — all normal; the last one just means this card stays short in your rotation.

    Out in the real world

    Corners are everywhere once you look: the edge of a picture frame, the zigzag of a knitted blanket, the chevron on a wet-floor sign at the shop. Name real corners casually and the card keeps echoing.

    Try it together

    Corner peek: trace to a corner, hide the card behind your palm for one second, then reveal it turned the other way. Tiny, safe, repeatable — the same surprise, packaged as peek-a-boo.

    Understanding check

    Self-check: did you mark the corners with your voice, and did the session end earlier than the wave session did? Both answers being yes means you read the card right — busy cards trade length for brightness.

    Parent tips

    If the zigzag floods your baby — darting eyes, stiff body, fussing — park it for a fortnight and stay with waves; there is no order to enforce. When it lands, it lands, and corners become the fun half of the set.

    Staying safe

    Busy cards can tip an alert baby into overload fast; watch for a pink face, flailing or gaze-darting and end at the first sign. Keep sound effects gentle — the tick-tock marks corners, it does not perform a concert.

    This lesson pairs with the Zigzag flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Faces & Visual Tracking (Newborn 2).

    LEARNING PATH LESSON · FACES & VISUAL TRACKING · AGES 6–12 WEEKS

    Large dots — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

    Not every card is a workout. The dots card is the set’s deep breath — and this lesson shows you how to use it as one.

    What is this?

    Large dots are just that: big, bold, round shapes with no corners and no direction. Nothing on this card moves or turns, which is precisely its gift — a place for young eyes to land and stay a while.

    What does it mean?

    After cards that ask the eyes to travel, a still image lets them settle. Visual rest is part of visual training: attention recovers on easy images, so the harder ones stay fun tomorrow. Dots are the nap of the set.

    What does the child need to know?

    Touch each dot with a fingertip as you count aloud — one, two, three. Your baby will not understand numbers for a long time yet; what lands is the rhythm and the steady, silly music of a voice that enjoys counting. The words are the melody, not the maths.

    Why this matters

    A baby who only ever meets high-energy input learns to need it; a baby who also meets calm images learns that quiet things are worth looking at too. Dots teach taste as much as vision — the plain can hold you.

    What it teaches

    Visual settling, attention recovery, early rhythm through counting aloud, and touch-eye pairing as your fingertip and your baby’s gaze meet on the same dot.

    Words to learn

    dotsroundonetwothreegentle

    Say this to your child

    “"Dots. Round as the moon, still as anything. One little dot... two little dots... three. All sitting still, waiting to be looked at. What a quiet, friendly card this is."”

    Step by step

    1. Show the card at resting distance — no performance needed — and say its name low and slow: "Dots. Big, round dots."
    2. Let the card simply be looked at for a while; this one does not need a job on day one.
    3. On the second visit, tap each dot once as you count aloud, unhurried: one... two... three.
    4. Tap them again tomorrow and the day after — same dots, same order, same calm voice. The repetition is the point.
    5. Let this card close sessions that started busy: one quiet minute of dots is a better ending than one more exciting card.

    Look closer at the picture

    The artwork gives you bold round shapes in a simple arrangement and nothing else — say that much, no stories. Then notice the thing that changes daily: does your baby’s breathing slow on this card? Settled bodies are the data here.

    Ask your child

    Watch for the settle: do small movements still, does breathing deepen, do the eyes rest on one dot or drift softly between them? Wonder aloud: "I wonder if this is the card you will want at bedtime."

    What your child can say or do

    Long soft staring, a body that goes heavy and still against you, slow blinking, or a first wobbly reach towards the nearest dot — at three months a reach is a rumour of the grab to come, and worth a cheer.

    Out in the real world

    Dots in the wild: buttons on a cardigan, the round end of a rattle, polka-dot sheets, the moon if the timing is kind. "Round like a dot" is a phrase that will follow your baby for years — plant it now.

    Try it together

    Dot kiss: touch your lips gently to your fingertip, then tap it on each dot with a soft kiss-noise, one per dot. Silly, calm, repeatable — and it attaches warmth to looking, which is the whole trick of this age.

    Understanding check

    Self-check: did the card get a full quiet minute, and did your own voice stay low the whole time? If the answer to the second is no, try again at the next feed — calm is caught from the holder, not taught.

    Parent tips

    Resist making dots exciting; their plainness is the feature. If your baby is frazzled, bring this card out first, not last. And if a sibling wants to run the counting, let them — a second voice doubles the rhythm practice for free.

    Staying safe

    A still, quiet card can drift a drowsy baby into sleep mid-session — lovely, but move the card away and settle them properly rather than leaving it alongside. Cards stay adult-held at this age, end of story.

    This lesson pairs with the Large dots flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Faces & Visual Tracking (Newborn 2).

    LEARNING PATH LESSON · FACES & VISUAL TRACKING · AGES 6–12 WEEKS

    Curved path — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

    This card has a beginning, a middle and an end, and this lesson is about travelling all three — slowly, with a small cheer waiting at the finish.

    What is this?

    A curved path is a single long line that sweeps across the card from one side to the other. Unlike the waves (many lines) or the rings (in and in), this is one road with one direction — a journey your baby’s eyes can complete.

    What does it mean?

    Following a line from start to finish is a chain of small visual decisions: stay on, keep going, arrive. Each completed run strengthens the habit of persistence in looking — and line-following is, one day, exactly what reading a sentence is.

    What does the child need to know?

    Slow matters more than finished. If the gaze drops off halfway, stop there and let the look be complete; a half journey today becomes a full one by next week. The small arrival cheer is for landings, however short the trip.

    Why this matters

    Every book your child will ever read runs on lines that go left to right and arrive somewhere. This card is that experience in its simplest costume — no letters, no story, just the pure pleasure of getting from here to there by eye.

    What it teaches

    Sustained line tracking, left-to-right direction, finish-and-celebrate sequencing, and shared attention — two people following the same path together.

    Words to learn

    pathlongstartendall the wayarrived

    Say this to your child

    “"One long, curvy path. Here is the start — off we go, slowly, slowly, all the way along... and here is the end! We arrived. What a journey for two small eyes and one patient finger."”

    Step by step

    1. Show the card and announce the journey: "A long curvy path — where does it go?"
    2. Put your fingertip at the line’s start and name it: "Here is the start." Then travel, slow as syrup, while the eyes ride along.
    3. If the gaze slips off, pause the finger where it slipped and wait; often the eyes climb back on by themselves.
    4. At the end, stop, lift your finger and mark the arrival with a small warm cheer — "arrived!" — every single time.
    5. Run it once more, or not, on your baby’s vote: a second full lap is a bonus, never a requirement.

    Look closer at the picture

    The artwork is one bold curved line sweeping across a plain card — that is the whole scene, so say that much. The noticing that matters is live: did today’s journey run further than yesterday’s? Progress here is measured in centimetres of attention.

    Ask your child

    Watch the trip: where does the gaze usually drop off — early, middle, near the end? Is that spot moving further along through the week? Wonder aloud: "I wonder if you will make it all the way by the weekend."

    What your child can say or do

    Eyes riding the finger for most of the line, a body-lean that follows the curve, a startle-smile at your arrival cheer, or a gaze that quits at the halfway hump — all four are fine, and the last one is simply where training starts.

    Out in the real world

    Paths are everywhere: the curve of the garden edge, a ribbon lying on the carpet, the S of a river on a map you glance at. Trace any long curve you meet — "long path... arrived" — and the card plays itself in the world.

    Try it together

    Ribbon run: lay a length of ribbon in a gentle curve on the floor beside your baby during tummy time and trace it with your finger, then let a sibling or partner walk a toy car along it. Same journey, new costume, twice the audience.

    Understanding check

    Self-check: did the finger actually travel the whole line at least once, and did you cheer the arrival even on a short run? The habit of finishing is built by celebrating finishes — yours to give, freely.

    Parent tips

    Vary which end you start from across the week, but keep most runs left to right — reading’s direction gets a quiet head start. If your baby always quits at the same spot, end the run there with the cheer anyway; arrival is wherever you stop together.

    Staying safe

    Tummy-time versions need full supervision, chin up, on a firm surface — a tracing session is no time to step away. Ribbon and string props live in your hand and go away with you; loose lengths near a baby are never left lying around.

    This lesson pairs with the Curved path flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Faces & Visual Tracking (Newborn 2).

    LEARNING PATH LESSON · FACES & VISUAL TRACKING · AGES 6–12 WEEKS

    Red circle — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

    Everything so far has been black and white. This card changes one thing — the colour — and this lesson shows you how to make that change visible without making it a lesson.

    What is this?

    Red opens the colour half of the set: one large, bold red circle on plain ground. Red happens to be the colour young eyes notice earliest, which makes this the classic first step out of the black-and-white world.

    What does it mean?

    Colour vision arrives in stages, and long-wavelength red registers before most of the spectrum. That is why generations of baby cards start here: the colour is new, but the odds of it landing are better than any other colour’s.

    What does the child need to know?

    The honest test: hold this card beside a black-and-white one and see whether the gaze travels to the red. Many babies go; some do not yet, and both are on schedule. The strong shape alone earns its keep while colour catches up.

    Why this matters

    A first colour is a first property: the same "circle-ness" wearing different clothes. Meeting that idea now, gently and repeatedly, prepares the ground for every colour word your child will one day sort the world into.

    What it teaches

    Colour noticing, comparison (colour against no-colour), choice behaviour when two cards compete, and the vocabulary seed of "red" said warmly and often.

    Words to learn

    redcircleroundcolourlookthere

    Say this to your child

    “"Red! Here is a big round circle, red as a berry. Look — next to it, a black and white one. Red... and not-red. Where will your eyes go? There they go. Red is a lovely thing to meet."”

    Step by step

    1. Show the red circle alone at focusing distance and name it with warmth: "Red. A big round circle in red."
    2. Say it a second time, slower, and let the card sit in view for a long moment before anything else happens.
    3. Now the experiment: bring a black-and-white card alongside and hold the pair steadily — equal heights, equal distances.
    4. Watch where the eyes settle or return. Whichever card wins, say so out loud — "you looked at the red!" — without scorekeeping.
    5. Repeat the pairing across a few days; colour noticing tends to arrive quietly between one session and the next.

    Look closer at the picture

    The artwork is one large red circle — say that plainly. The comparison is where the noticing lives: does the red pull the gaze across, or does the familiar black-and-white hold it? Either outcome tells you something true about this week.

    Ask your child

    Watch the crossing: does the gaze visit the red card first, return to it, or stay put on the black and white? Wonder aloud: "I wonder if red looks loud or quiet to you this month."

    What your child can say or do

    A direct gaze-lock on the red, back-and-forth comparing between the two cards, a fresh burst of interest after days of black-and-white familiarity, or total indifference — the last one is schedule, not failure.

    Out in the real world

    Red shows up for babies more than you would guess: a red mug, the cover of a board book, a red jumper folded in the pushchair basket. Tap each real red once and say the word — the card travels with you.

    Try it together

    Red hunt, parent edition: before the session, find two or three red things and lay them near the card. Name the card, then each real red in turn, one tap each. The world, briefly, is organised around one colour — and your baby gets to watch you enjoy it.

    Understanding check

    Self-check: did the red-versus-black-and-white comparison actually happen this week, and did you say "red" warmly at least a handful of times? Both are cheap to do, and the pairing is the lesson’s engine.

    Parent tips

    If red earns nothing, keep the card in rotation anyway — the shape is doing quiet work while colour waits its turn. Offer one colour at a time across the set; three colours at once is three chances to teach nothing.

    Staying safe

    Colour talk invites pointing at the world — fine, because your finger does the pointing. Keep the card itself out of the grab-and-gum zone unless you are holding it; wet cards fray, and frayed cards go in the bin, not the mouth.

    This lesson pairs with the Red circle flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Faces & Visual Tracking (Newborn 2).

    LEARNING PATH LESSON · FACES & VISUAL TRACKING · AGES 6–12 WEEKS

    Red and black — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

    This card refuses to choose: bold black and strong red share the page. This lesson uses the mixture to name parts, sort aloud and let your baby’s eyes do the filing.

    What is this?

    A red-and-black card joins the two visual worlds your baby now lives between — the high contrast they have known for weeks and the colour they met in the last card. Same boldness, two inks, one image.

    What does it mean?

    Mixed cards are stepping stones by design. The black keeps the contrast signal strong while the red rides along inside the same picture, so colour gets rehearsed in the most comfortable format a young eye knows.

    What does the child need to know?

    Your finger is the sorter: touch a red part and name it, touch a black part and name it, taking turns. The sorting is yours to perform aloud — your baby supplies the looking, and the looking is the learning.

    Why this matters

    Part-naming is the seed of every later description — red wheel, black wheel, big dog, small dog. An image that comes in two clear parts makes the part-and-name game easy to run and easy to repeat.

    What it teaches

    Part-whole perception, colour naming in narration, visual sorting by following your touch, and steady shared attention on one multi-part image.

    Words to learn

    redblackpartherethereboth

    Say this to your child

    “"Red and black! This part is red... and this part is black. Red here, black there, red and black sharing one card. Two colours, one picture, and your eyes seeing both at once. Clever eyes."”

    Step by step

    1. Show the card at focusing distance and give it its honest name: "Red and black together."
    2. Trace the red parts first, one slow touch each, saying red every time your finger lands.
    3. Then tour the black parts the same way — black, black, black — at the same unhurried speed.
    4. Mix the order on the second lap: red, black, red, black, so the eyes start jumping between the two.
    5. End with the whole card in one view and one summary line — "red and black, all on one card" — then stop talking and let the looking finish the session.

    Look closer at the picture

    The artwork lays red shapes against solid black shapes on one card — describe that much and move on. The richer noticing is behavioural: does your baby’s gaze jump when you jump, from red part to black part? Following your finger is joint attention arriving on schedule.

    Ask your child

    Watch the jumps: does the gaze shadow each touch, or wander off on its own route? Does one colour collect more looking? Wonder aloud: "I wonder if the red parts feel louder to you, or just newer."

    What your child can say or do

    Eyes that follow your fingertip part by part, a longer look at one colour’s territory, soft babbling that answers your naming rhythm, or a hand batting towards the card mid-lap — each is a version of "I see what you are doing".

    Out in the real world

    The pairing is everywhere: a red toy on a dark rug, red letters on a black sign, ladybirds on the lawn. Wherever red sits against dark, a two-second "red and black" keeps this card echoing through the week.

    Try it together

    Two-hands game: one hand touches a red part, the other a black part, taking turns — and your baby’s eyes swing between them like a slow tennis match. Two players, one card, zero equipment.

    Understanding check

    Self-check: did you name parts in turns rather than all at once, and did your baby’s gaze make at least one clear jump between colours? The turn-taking is your half; the jumping is theirs — both count.

    Parent tips

    Keep the naming rhythm slower than speech — this is dictation for the eyes. If your baby prefers one colour’s territory, follow their lead and start there next time; preference is fuel, not a problem.

    Staying safe

    This is a look-and-touch card, so it will attract hands eventually — let grabs happen against your held card, not against a propped one. Inspect the card after any gumming; soft corners get retired before they can flake.

    This lesson pairs with the Red and black flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Faces & Visual Tracking (Newborn 2).

    LEARNING PATH LESSON · FACES & VISUAL TRACKING · AGES 6–12 WEEKS

    Red face detail — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

    The last card of the set brings everything back: a face, bold shapes, and a patch of red. This lesson uses it the way finales work — as the calm, warm ending your sessions deserve.

    What is this?

    A friendly face carrying a splash of red, drawn in the same high-contrast style as the rest of the set. It gathers the stage’s three threads — faces, patterns, colour — into a single image and makes a natural last card of the day.

    What does it mean?

    Endings shape memories, for babies as for everyone. A finisher card that combines the familiar (a face) with the newest thing (red) lets a session close on both comfort and novelty — the mix that keeps looking fresh without overload.

    What does the child need to know?

    The running order is the trick: tour the face parts first and keep the red patch for the very last touch. Ending on the newest element gives it the best chance of being noticed, and gives the session a built-in final scene.

    Why this matters

    A predictable ending teaches your baby the shape of a session — things begin, things are enjoyed, things end warmly. Babies who know how sessions end come back to the next one more easily. The ritual is the lesson beneath the lesson.

    What it teaches

    Sequencing (parts first, detail last), consolidation — this card quietly reviews the whole set — and the emotional rhythm of a calm, predictable finish.

    Words to learn

    faceredlastfinishtomorrowbye

    Say this to your child

    “"Here is our last look: a friendly face with a bit of red. Eyes first, mouth next... and red, last of all, like a bow on a present. Card time is done. We will look again tomorrow, little one."”

    Step by step

    1. Settle into a calm moment and show the card with a slower voice than usual: "Last card of the day. A face, with red."
    2. Tour the face parts first — eyes, mouth, whatever the drawing offers — one warm touch each, in no hurry.
    3. Save the red detail for the final touch: land on it, name it, and let your finger rest there a beat longer than the rest.
    4. Say one closing line to your baby — "card time is finished; we had a lovely look" — so endings get words as well as feelings.
    5. Put the cards away together, visibly. What is tidied away returns tomorrow; that promise is part of the ritual.

    Look closer at the picture

    The artwork is a bold face carrying a red detail — describe exactly that much and no more. The noticing worth keeping is yours to gather: how long did the final session run, and did the red get the last look? Those two facts are your stage report.

    Ask your child

    Watch the close: does your baby’s attention hold through the face tour and sharpen at the red? Does the closing line — the same one each time — begin to signal "finished"? Wonder aloud: "I wonder when you will start relaxing at that exact sentence."

    What your child can say or do

    A final round of steady looking, a softening of the whole body as the voice slows, a smile at the familiar closing words, or eyes that leave the card before the red arrives — the session still counts; endings do not need full attendance.

    Out in the real world

    Rituals of ending run through every baby day: the last feed before the nap, the sleep-sack zip, the light going off with a goodbye to the room. This card gives looking-time its own version of the same gentle close.

    Try it together

    Goodbye lap: on the final pass, whisper a tiny goodbye to each part — "bye, eyes... bye, mouth... bye, red" — always ending on the red. Within weeks the whisper itself will start the softening; that is conditioning in its kindest form.

    Understanding check

    Self-check: did the session end deliberately — with the closing line and the tidy-away — rather than trailing off into fussing? Deliberate endings are the difference between a class and a habit you will regret.

    Parent tips

    Keep the closing ritual identical every time — same words, same order, red last. Predictability is what turns a pile of cards into a class your baby recognises. When the set restarts next week, it will feel like a new class; that is by design.

    Staying safe

    Endings matter for safety too: cards go away with you, out of cot and reach, every single time. A finisher card is still paper to a baby — the ritual that ends with tidy-up is the ritual that keeps everyone safe.

    This lesson pairs with the Red face detail flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Faces & Visual Tracking (Newborn 2).
